etymology: From sports standings, where L marks a loss and W a win. "Take the L" (accept the loss) circulated in hip-hop and sports talk through the 2000s–2010s and became a Gen-Z and gaming staple; to "take an L" is to suffer a defeat or embarrassment, and to "take the L" is to admit it. Often shortened to just "L" as a verdict ("that’s an L").
biblical_def: In current slang to take the L is to accept a loss — a game, an argument, a rejection, an embarrassment — and move on, ideally without making excuses. "Just take the L, bro." As a habit it is surprisingly close to wisdom. The Christian observation: Scripture expects God’s people to lose, and to know how. "A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again" (Pro 24:16); "when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me" (Mic 7:8). Taking the L humbly is what Peter commands: "Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time" (1Pe 5:6). But the gospel turns the phrase inside out. Christ’s whole call is to take the L on purpose: "whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it" (Mat 16:25). Paul tallied his whole résumé and wrote it all in the loss column: "what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ" (Php 3:7). The cross looked like the greatest L in history and was the decisive W. A father tells his son: learn to lose a game without sulking and an argument without lying; and learn the bigger thing — that the man who will not lose anything for Christ loses everything, and the man who loses everything for Christ wins Him.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (sports and hip-hop; general 2010s) for accepting a loss without excuse — a humble habit Scripture commends, and a picture of the Christian life: losing for Christ to find life.
webster_full: TAKE THE L, v. phr. (Gen-Z slang; from sports W–L records) To accept a loss, defeat, or embarrassment. "She said no. Just take the L."
Take an L, to suffer a loss; L alone as a verdict: "that’s an L," "massive L." Opposite: W, dub.
Gaming use: concede, move to the next match.

Webster (1828), root word loss: “LOSS, noun 1. privation, as the loss of property; loss of money by gaming; loss of health or reputation. every loss is not a detriment. we cannot regret the loss of bad company or of evil habits. 2. Destruction; ruin; as the loss of a ship at sea; the loss of an army. 3. Defeat; as the loss of a battle. 4. Waste; useless application;”
Decode for parents: a good phrase to borrow when teaching children to lose well.
scriptures: For a just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again: but the wicked shall fall into mischief.
Mic 7:8
Rejoice not against me, O mine enemy: when I fall, I shall arise; when I sit in darkness, the LORD shall be a light unto me.
Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time:
For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it.
Php 3:7
But what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ.
corruption_summary: Take the L teaches a sound habit — admit defeat and move on; its only limit is that it treats loss as something to shrug off, where Scripture teaches losing for Christ as the way to life.
corruption_paragraphs: Little needs correcting here; the phrase is a small sermon against excuses. A boy who can say "I lost, my fault" is learning something many grown men never do. Proverbs builds the same muscle: the just man falls seven times and gets up again (Pro 24:16), and Peter commands humility under God’s hand (1Pe 5:6).

The gospel goes further than the slang. The world takes Ls reluctantly and hopes for Ws; Christ calls His followers to choose the loss: "whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it" (Mat 16:25). Paul put his pedigree, his learning, and his reputation in the loss column "for Christ" (Php 3:7). Teach your children to lose well at checkers so they can lose everything well for Him.
roots_summary: Sports W–L records → hip-hop and sports talk "take the L" (2000s) → Gen-Z and gaming staple; "L" as a one-letter verdict.
roots_lines: 2000s–2010s hip-hop and sports media: "take the L"
usage: "Missed the shot, lost the game. I’ll take the L."
A just man falleth seven times, and riseth up again (Pro 24:16).
Whosoever will lose his life for Christ shall find it (Mat 16:25).

etymology: From the spoken name of the letter W ("double-u," shortened to "dub"), the win column in sports records. "Get the dub" and "take the dub" spread through sports talk, hip-hop, and especially Fortnite and other online games in the late 2010s. Distinct from the older verbs dub (to knight; to name) and dub (to add a soundtrack or translation).
biblical_def: In current slang a dub is a win: a victory in a game, a good grade, a small success. "We got the dub." "Huge dub." It is the opposite of an L. The Christian observation: Scripture is not shy about victory. The Psalms celebrate battles won, Paul uses athletic contests freely — "So run, that ye may obtain" (1Co 9:24) — and the Christian is "more than conquerors through him that loved us" (Rom 8:37). Wanting to win is not a sin. But Scripture is careful about whose dub it is. The race is not finally "to the swift, nor the battle to the strong... but time and chance happeneth to them all" (Ecc 9:11); every earthly win is a gift and a temporary one. Paul contrasts the athlete’s "corruptible crown" with the believer’s "incorruptible" one (1Co 9:25). And the greatest dub is not ours at all: "thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ" (1Co 15:57); "this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith" (1Jn 5:4). A father celebrates his son’s dubs on the field and teaches him to say thank you for them — and to remember the one victory that cannot be lost.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (from "double-u," the W of a win record; gaming, late 2010s) for a win — victories Scripture celebrates as gifts, beneath the victory God gives in Christ.
webster_full: DUB, n. (Gen-Z slang; from the letter W, "double-u") A win, a victory, a success. "Got the dub tonight." "That’s a huge dub."
Also W alone: "W," "big W," "W friend." Opposite: L (see Take the L).
Older, unrelated senses: dub, to confer knighthood or a name; to add sound to film; British dubs, twenty-inch wheels.

Webster (1828), root word dub: “DUB, verb transitive […] Literally, to strike. Hence, 1. To strike a blow with a sword, and make a knight. Se cyng, dubbade his sunu Henric to ridere. The King dubbed his son Henry a knight. 2. To confer any dignity or new character. A man of wealth is dubbd a man of worth.”
Decode for parents: a win. Celebrate it, and teach thanksgiving for it.
scriptures: But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Rom 8:37
Nay, in all these things we are more than conquerors through him that loved us.
For whatsoever is born of God overcometh the world: and this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith.
Ecc 9:11

I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all.
And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible.
corruption_summary: Dub is honest delight in winning; its drift is only the scoreboard heart that lives for the next W, where Scripture receives every win as a gift and rests in the victory God gives in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Winning is good, and Scripture uses races and contests to describe the Christian life (1Co 9:24–25). The drift is a heart that measures every day in Ws and Ls — ranked matches, likes, grades, girls — and feels worthless after a loss. The Preacher punctured that long ago: the race is not always to the swift, "but time and chance happeneth to them all" (Ecc 9:11).

The believer has a win that is not on the board. "Thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory" (1Co 15:57); "this is the victory that overcometh the world, even our faith" (1Jn 5:4). Teach your son to chase dubs hard, to thank God for each one, and to know that his biggest dub was won for him.
roots_summary: Letter W ("double-u") in sports records → spoken "dub" → hip-hop, sports talk, Fortnite (late 2010s) → Gen-Z word for any win.
roots_lines: The letter W, spoken "double-u"; win column in standings
Clipped to "dub" in sports and hip-hop talk
Late 2010s: Fortnite and online gaming spread "get the dub"
Distinct from dub, to knight or to name (Old English dubbian)
usage: "Aced the chem test. Dub."
Thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory (1Co 15:57).
They run for a corruptible crown; we an incorruptible (1Co 9:25).

etymology: Gaming slang, widespread from about 2020–2021 in online multiplayer and streaming chat: when a player blames lag, the controller, or the game for a loss, others reply "skill issue" — the problem is you. It spread to Twitter and everyday Gen-Z speech as a dismissive retort to any complaint.
biblical_def: In current slang skill issue is the two-word comeback to any excuse: you lost because you are not good enough, not because of the lag. It is mostly a taunt, sometimes a fair point. The Christian observation: there is a hard truth in the jab. Scripture does tell us to own our failures instead of blaming the controller: "every man shall bear his own burden" (Gal 6:5). Skill matters to God; David shepherded Israel "by the skilfulness of his hands" (Psa 78:72), and Proverbs promises that "a man diligent in his business... shall stand before kings" (Pro 22:29). Practice is wisdom: "If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct" (Ecc 10:10). But the slang is used to mock, and Paul gives the opposite instruction for a brother who fails: "restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted" (Gal 6:1), and "Bear ye one another’s burdens" (Gal 6:2). And the deepest human problem is not a skill issue at all. Sin is not fixed by grinding; it is forgiven by grace. A father can use the phrase on himself ("my fault, skill issue") and teach his son to say it about his own failures while helping, not mocking, others with theirs.
webster_summary: Gaming slang (c. 2020–2021) meaning "your failure is your own fault" — a true word about owning failure, used as a taunt; Scripture says bear your own burden and restore others in meekness.
webster_full: SKILL ISSUE, n. phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present; gaming origin) Retort to an excuse: the failure is due to lack of skill, not circumstances. "The game’s rigged!" "Skill issue."
Extended to any complaint: homework, sports, dating.
Self-deprecating use: "I burned the toast. Skill issue."
Webster (1828), root word skill: “SKILL, verb intransitive 1. To be knowing in; to be dextrous in performance. 2. To differ; to make difference; to matter or be of interest.”
Decode for parents: a taunt with a grain of truth. Teach the truth, drop the taunt.
scriptures: Gal 6:5
For every man shall bear his own burden.
If the iron be blunt, and he do not whet the edge, then must he put to more strength: but wisdom is profitable to direct.
Seest thou a man diligent in his business? he shall stand before kings; he shall not stand before mean men.
Gal 6:1
Brethren, if a man be overtaken in a fault, ye which are spiritual, restore such an one in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself, lest thou also be tempted.
Gal 6:2
Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.
corruption_summary: Skill issue rightly refuses excuses and wrongly mocks the one who failed; Scripture keeps the responsibility (Gal 6:5) and replaces the taunt with restoring the fallen in meekness (Gal 6:1).
corruption_paragraphs: The phrase has a moral spine: stop blaming the lag. Scripture agrees that a man must own his failures (Gal 6:5) and sharpen his axe instead of complaining that it is dull (Ecc 10:10). Many teenagers need exactly this word about their grades, chores, and habits.

But the slang is aimed outward, as a sneer. Paul aims it inward and turns the outward posture into mercy: restore the one overtaken in a fault "in the spirit of meekness; considering thyself" (Gal 6:1). And remind your children that their deepest failure is not a skill issue. No amount of practice removes sin; Christ does.
roots_summary: Skill + issue → c. 2020–2021 multiplayer gaming and stream chat → Twitter meme → general Gen-Z retort to excuses.
roots_lines: Online multiplayer: excuses about lag, hitboxes, controllers
Self-deprecating use for one’s own mistakes
usage: "Couldn’t beat the boss? Skill issue."
Bear your own burden (Gal 6:5) — and help bear your brother’s (Gal 6:2).
Whet the edge; wisdom is profitable to direct (Ecc 10:10).

etymology: A blend of grind (hard, relentless work, from 19th-century student slang and 2000s hip-hop "on the grind") and mindset. "Sigma male grindset" memes appeared around 2020–2021, partly parodying and partly promoting the hustle-influencer gospel of 4 a.m. alarms, cold plunges, no days off, and money as the measure of a man. Associated with the manosphere and figures such as Andrew Tate.
biblical_def: In current slang the grindset is the mindset of relentless work toward money and status: wake at four, no days off, cut out friends who slow you down, rest is for losers. Teen boys meet it in memes that are half-joke, half-creed. The Christian observation: Scripture honours hard work; "Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work" (Exo 20:9). But it also commands the seventh day: "in it thou shalt not do any work" (Exo 20:10). The grindset abolishes the Sabbath and calls the result virtue. The Preacher described its endpoint exactly: a man alone, "yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches; neither saith he, For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good?" (Ecc 4:8). "It is vain for you to rise up early, to sit up late, to eat the bread of sorrows: for so he giveth his beloved sleep" (Psa 127:2). "Labour not to be rich" (Pro 23:4). And Jesus asks the question no grindset meme asks: "what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?" (Mat 16:26). A father tells his son: work hard, harder than the meme guys; and rest one day in seven, love your family, and sleep, because your life is a gift from God, not a startup.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (meme, c. 2020–2021; "sigma grindset") for a mindset of relentless work toward money and status — diligence without Sabbath, which Scripture calls vanity and a sore travail.
webster_full: GRINDSET, n. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present; blend of grind + mindset) A mindset of relentless, sacrificial work for money and status. "No days off. Grindset."
Common in "sigma male grindset" memes, both sincere and parodic.
Tenets: early alarms, cold showers, cutting off "distractions," money as the score.

Webster (1828), root word grind: “GRIND, verb transitive preterit tense and participle passive ground. […] 1. To break and reduce to fine particles or powder by friction; to comminute by attrition; to triturate. Take the millstones and grind meal. Isaiah 47:2. We say, to grind meal, but this is an elliptical phrase. The true phrase is, to grind corn to meal. 2.”
Decode for parents: your son may be absorbing a creed that abolishes rest. Teach work and Sabbath together.
scriptures: Exo 20:9
Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work:

But the seventh day is the sabbath of the LORD thy God: in it thou shalt not do any work, thou, nor thy son, nor thy daughter, thy manservant, nor thy maidservant, nor thy cattle, nor thy stranger that is within thy gates:
Ecc 4:8

There is one alone, and there is not a second; yea, he hath neither child nor brother: yet is there no end of all his labour; neither is his eye satisfied with riches; neither saith he, For whom do I labour, and bereave my soul of good? This is also vanity, yea, it is a sore travail.
Pro 23:4
Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom.
For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?
corruption_summary: Grindset baptizes work without rest and money as the measure of a man; Scripture commands six days of labour and one of rest, and calls endless labour for riches vanity and a sore travail.
corruption_paragraphs: The grindset gets one commandment right and breaks the next. Work is good; six days of labour is God’s own order (Exo 20:9). But the creed has no seventh day, no family, no sleep, and no answer to the question "for whom do I labour?" (Ecc 4:8). It is the Preacher’s lonely rich man, sold to teenage boys as a lifestyle brand.

The gospel gives a man something the grindset cannot: a reason to stop. "So he giveth his beloved sleep" (Psa 127:2). Rest is an act of faith that God, not my hustle, holds the world together. Teach your son to outwork the meme crowd and to keep the Sabbath; to provide for his house and to ask what it profits to gain the world and lose his soul (Mat 16:26).
roots_summary: Grind (hard work; hip-hop "on the grind") + mindset → c. 2020–2021 "sigma male grindset" memes → Gen-Z word for the hustle creed.
roots_lines: Old English grindan — to crush between stones
c. 2020–2021: "sigma male grindset" memes, manosphere influencers
usage: "Four a.m. workout, no weekends. Grindset."
Six days labour; the seventh is the Sabbath of the LORD (Exo 20:9–10).
What is a man profited, if he gain the whole world? (Mat 16:26)

etymology: From hip-hop bag, a bag of money (a large sum; also a big contract). "Secure the bag" and "get the bag" were common in 2010s rap and sports talk (athletes "securing the bag" with a big contract), and by about 2017–2018 Gen-Z used it for getting money of any kind — a job, a deal, a payment. "Fumble the bag" means to lose an opportunity.
biblical_def: In current slang to secure the bag is to get the money: land the job, sign the contract, close the deal. It is often said with admiration and a hint that money is the point of everything. The Christian observation: Scripture has an exact image for this, and it is a warning. Haggai describes a people who worked hard and prospered on paper, but "he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes" (Hag 1:6). Every earthly bag leaks. Jesus tells of a man who secured the biggest bag of his life — barns full — and God said, "Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee" (Luk 12:20); "So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God" (Luk 12:21). Then He offers the better bag: "provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not" (Luk 12:33). Earning is not wrong — a man who will not provide for his house is worse than an infidel — but "they that will be rich fall into temptation and a snare" (1Ti 6:9), and "the love of money is the root of all evil" (1Ti 6:10). A father tells his son: secure the bag for your family and your giving, and secure the bag that does not wax old first.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (hip-hop, 2010s) for getting the money — a phrase Scripture answers with Haggai’s bag with holes and Christ’s bags which wax not old.
webster_full: SECURE THE BAG, v. phr. (Gen-Z slang; hip-hop and sports origin, 2010s) To obtain money, especially a large payment, contract, or job. "Got the internship. Secured the bag."
Variants: get the bag, chase the bag; fumble the bag, to lose an opportunity.
Bag alone: a large sum of money.

Webster (1828), nearest root purse: “PURSE, noun purs. […] 1. A small bag in which money is contained or carried in the pocket. It was formerly made of leather, and is still made of this material by common people. It is usually of silk net-work. 2. A sum of money offered as the prize of winning in a horse race. 3.”
Decode for parents: ambition about money. Teach provision, generosity, and the bag that does not leak.
scriptures: Hag 1:6

Ye have sown much, and bring in little; ye eat, but ye have not enough; ye drink, but ye are not filled with drink; ye clothe you, but there is none warm; and he that earneth wages earneth wages to put it into a bag with holes.
But God said unto him, Thou fool, this night thy soul shall be required of thee: then whose shall those things be, which thou hast provided?
So is he that layeth up treasure for himself, and is not rich toward God.
Sell that ye have, and give alms; provide yourselves bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens that faileth not, where no thief approacheth, neither moth corrupteth.
For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows.
corruption_summary: Secure the bag treats money as the prize of life; Scripture says every earthly bag has holes (Hag 1:6) and Christ commands the bag which waxes not old (Luk 12:33).
corruption_paragraphs: Providing is a duty, and a young man eager to earn is better than one content to drift. The corruption is the assumption under the phrase: that the bag is the goal and the self is the beneficiary. Jesus’s rich fool secured the bag perfectly and was called a fool the same night (Luk 12:20), because he was "not rich toward God" (Luk 12:21).

Haggai saw the leak: wages put "into a bag with holes" (Hag 1:6) when God’s house is neglected. Christ offers the only bag that holds: "bags which wax not old, a treasure in the heavens" (Luk 12:33), filled by giving, not grabbing. Teach your son to earn, tithe, save, give, and to fear the love of money more than poverty (1Ti 6:10).
roots_summary: Hip-hop bag (a large sum of money) → 2010s rap and sports contract talk "secure the bag" → c. 2017–2018 Gen-Z general use; "fumble the bag."
roots_lines: Hip-hop bag — a bag of money; a large payment
2010s sports media: athletes "securing the bag" in contracts
c. 2017–2018: general Gen-Z use for any earning
usage: "Took the extra shifts to secure the bag."
Wages into a bag with holes (Hag 1:6).
Provide yourselves bags which wax not old (Luk 12:33).

etymology: From British and American slang cop, to catch or seize (18th century; the policeman is a copper, one who cops criminals). African-American English used cop for obtaining something, especially buying, by the mid-20th century; sneaker and streetwear culture of the 2000s–2010s made it standard: to cop a release is to buy it, and "cop or drop?" asks whether an item is worth buying.
biblical_def: In current slang to cop something is to buy it, usually something wanted and limited: sneakers, a hoodie, tickets. "I’m copping these." "Cop or drop?" It is the verb of acquisition in a culture of drops and releases. The Christian observation: buying is not sin. The woman of Proverbs "considereth a field, and buyeth it" (Pro 31:16) — a thoughtful cop. But Scripture asks the question the slang skips: why buy this? "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not?" (Isa 55:2). The same chapter offers the strangest purchase ever advertised: "come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price" (Isa 55:1) — grace is the one thing you cannot cop, only receive. Jesus warns, "a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth" (Luk 12:15), and Paul tells believers to buy "as though they possessed not... for the fashion of this world passeth away" (1Co 7:30–31). The best cop in Revelation is Christ’s counsel: "buy of me gold tried in the fire" (Rev 3:18). A father can teach his son to ask "cop or drop" seriously: is it bread, or that which satisfies not?
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (from cop, to seize; sneaker culture 2000s–2010s) for buying something wanted — acquisition Scripture questions: why spend for that which is not bread?
webster_full: COP, v.t. (Gen-Z slang; AAVE and sneaker-culture origin) To buy or obtain, especially a desired or limited item. "Finally copped the Jordans."
Cop or drop — should I buy it or pass? Copped, bought.
Older slang: to catch, seize (hence copper, cop, a policeman); cop out, to evade.

Webster (1828), root word cop: “COP, noun […] The had or top of a thing, as in cob-castle for cop-castle, a castle on a hill; a tuft on the head of birds. This word is Little Used in America, unless cob, the spike of maize, may be the same word.”
Decode for parents: the language of buying. Ask the "cop or drop" question together.
scriptures: Isa 55:2

Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread? and your labour for that which satisfieth not? hearken diligently unto me, and eat ye that which is good, and let your soul delight itself in fatness.
Isa 55:1
Ho, every one that thirsteth, come ye to the waters, and he that hath no money; come ye, buy, and eat; yea, come, buy wine and milk without money and without price.
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
And they that use this world, as not abusing it: for the fashion of this world passeth away.
Rev 3:18

I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed, and that the shame of thy nakedness do not appear; and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.
corruption_summary: Cop makes acquisition the reflex of a drop-driven culture; Scripture permits buying, asks why we spend for that which is not bread, and offers grace that cannot be bought.
corruption_paragraphs: The sneaker drop is a small liturgy: the countdown, the app, the rush, the "copped" post. It trains a teenager to want on schedule and to feel that having is the point. Jesus cuts against the whole rhythm: "a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth" (Luk 12:15).

Isaiah’s market is the true one. "Wherefore do ye spend money for that which is not bread?" (Isa 55:2) — and then the offer: "buy wine and milk without money and without price" (Isa 55:1). Christ counsels us to buy from Him "gold tried in the fire" (Rev 3:18). Teach your children to cop thoughtfully, drop often, and receive freely the one thing money cannot buy.
roots_summary: 18th-c. slang cop (to catch, seize) → AAVE cop, to obtain or buy → 2000s–2010s sneaker culture "cop or drop" → Gen-Z verb for buying.
roots_lines: Possibly from Old French caper or Dutch kapen — to seize
Mid-20th c. AAVE: cop, to obtain or buy
2000s–2010s sneaker and streetwear culture: "cop or drop"
Gen-Z: any purchase of something wanted
usage: "They restocked the hoodie. Cop or drop?"
Why spend money for that which is not bread? (Isa 55:2)
Buy of Me gold tried in the fire (Rev 3:18).

etymology: From the Holy Grail of medieval Arthurian romance (12th–13th centuries, Chrétien de Troyes and later writers), the legendary cup of the Last Supper sought by the knights. "Holy grail" for any ultimate goal is long-standing English; collector and sneaker culture of the 2000s–2010s shortened it to grail: the one item a collector most wants ("my grail sneakers"). Gen-Z extends it to any dream possession.
biblical_def: In current slang a grail is the item you most want and have hunted longest: the rare sneaker, the vintage jacket, the first-edition card. Collectors keep "grail lists," and getting one is a life event. The Christian observation: the word carries a story it has forgotten. The medieval Grail was a quest for the cup of Christ’s own Supper — a quest for holiness, which only the pure could finish. The slang keeps the longing and swaps the object for merchandise. Jesus told a story about exactly this kind of collector: "a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it" (Mat 13:45–46). That is the true grail — the kingdom of heaven — and it is worth more than everything else on the list. Everything else disappoints on arrival: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver" (Ecc 5:10). The test is Christ’s: "where your treasure is, there will your heart be also" (Mat 6:21). A father can enjoy his son’s collection and ask him for his real grail list — and pray with him the psalmist’s answer: "Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee" (Psa 73:25).
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (collector culture, from the Holy Grail) for one’s most-wanted possession — a longing Christ points to the one pearl of great price.
webster_full: GRAIL, n. (Gen-Z slang; collector and sneaker culture, 2000s–present) The item a collector most desires; a dream possession. "Found my grail at a thrift store."
Grail list, a ranked list of most-wanted items; grail as adj.: "grail pair."
From Holy Grail, the legendary cup of the Last Supper sought by Arthur’s knights; figuratively any ultimate goal.
Webster (1828), root word grail: “GRAIL, noun […] A book of offices in the Romish church.”
Decode for parents: ask your child what is on his grail list, and what is at the top of his heart’s.
scriptures: Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:
Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
Ecc 5:10
He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver; nor he that loveth abundance with increase: this is also vanity.
Mat 6:21
For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also.
Whom have I in heaven but thee? and there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee.
corruption_summary: Grail keeps the language of a holy quest and spends it on merchandise; Christ names the true grail — the pearl of great price, worth selling everything for.
corruption_paragraphs: A word that once meant the cup of the Lord’s Supper now means a pair of shoes. The shift is a small parable of an age that still feels the longing for something ultimate but has nothing ultimate to aim it at. So the longing settles on objects, and each grail, once found, becomes a shelf item and the search moves on: "He that loveth silver shall not be satisfied with silver" (Ecc 5:10).

Jesus honours the collector’s instinct and redirects it. The merchant who found "one pearl of great price" sold everything for it (Mat 13:46). That pearl is the kingdom, and its King is the only grail who satisfies on arrival. Teach your children to say with Asaph, "there is none upon earth that I desire beside thee" (Psa 73:25).
roots_summary: Medieval Latin gradalis (a dish) → Old French graal → Arthurian Holy Grail → "holy grail," an ultimate goal → collector slang grail.
roots_lines: Medieval Latin gradalis — a dish or platter
12th–13th c. Arthurian romance: the Holy Grail, cup of the Last Supper
English "holy grail" — any ultimate object of a quest
usage: "Those vintage cleats are my grail."
The true grail: one pearl of great price (Mat 13:46).
None upon earth that I desire beside Thee (Psa 73:25).

etymology: From hype (excited promotion, 1920s American slang from hyperbole) and beast. Hypebeast was the name of a streetwear blog founded by Kevin Ma in Hong Kong in 2005, and in the 2010s it became a label, often mocking, for someone who chases whatever streetwear and sneaker brands are hyped — Supreme, Yeezy, Off-White — buying for status rather than taste.
biblical_def: In current slang a hypebeast is a person, usually a teenage boy, who must have whatever is hyped: the newest drop, the logo, the resale-value sneaker, worn to be seen. The word is mostly an insult, which shows that even the culture knows something is off. The Christian observation: Scripture’s word for this is covetousness, and the tenth commandment addresses it directly: "Thou shalt not covet... any thing that is thy neighbour’s" (Exo 20:17). The hypebeast covets not a neighbour’s house but his neighbour’s attention. John names the triad underneath: "the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world" (1Jn 2:16) — and adds the sentence that ends every hype cycle: "the world passeth away, and the lust thereof" (1Jn 2:17). The Preacher knew the treadmill: "the eye is not satisfied with seeing" (Ecc 1:8). Jesus warns, "Take heed, and beware of covetousness" (Luk 12:15). And Hebrews gives the cure: "be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee" (Heb 13:5). A father tells his son: buy good things and wear them long; do not let the brand tell you who you are; the man secure in Christ does not need the hype.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (from the 2005 streetwear blog Hypebeast) for one who chases hyped brands for status — covetousness and the pride of life, which pass away with the drop.
webster_full: HYPEBEAST, n. (Gen-Z slang, 2010s–present; from the 2005 blog of that name) One who obsessively buys hyped streetwear and sneakers for status. "Total hypebeast — logos head to toe."
Usually derisive; sometimes worn as a badge.
Kin terms: sneakerhead (a collector, often more knowledgeable), reseller.

Webster (1828), nearest root hyperbole: “HYPER'BOLE, noun hyper'boly. […] In rhetoric, a figure of speech which expresses much more or less than the truth, or which represents things much greater or less, better or worse than they really are.”
Decode for parents: covetousness with a logo. Teach contentment and long-worn, well-chosen things.
scriptures: Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house, thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his manservant, nor his maidservant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor any thing that is thy neighbour's.
For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, and the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, is not of the Father, but is of the world.
And the world passeth away, and the lust thereof: but he that doeth the will of God abideth for ever.
Ecc 1:8
All things are full of labour; man cannot utter it: the eye is not satisfied with seeing, nor the ear filled with hearing.
Heb 13:5
Let your conversation be without covetousness; and be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee, nor forsake thee.
corruption_summary: Hypebeast names covetousness worn as identity — the lust of the eyes and the pride of life chasing the next drop; Scripture answers with the tenth commandment and contentment in Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The hypebeast is the tenth commandment broken in public. He wants what others want because others want it; the value is the hype, and the hype is someone else’s attention. John’s triad fits exactly — "the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life" (1Jn 2:16) — and so does his epitaph: "the world passeth away, and the lust thereof" (1Jn 2:17). Every drop is obsolete in a season.

The cure is not ugly clothes but a settled heart. "Be content with such things as ye have: for he hath said, I will never leave thee" (Heb 13:5). A boy who knows he is held by Christ does not need a logo to tell the hallway who he is. Teach your son to buy well, wear long, and laugh at the hype.
roots_summary: Hype (from hyperbole, 1920s) + beast → 2005 Hong Kong streetwear blog Hypebeast → 2010s label for status-driven streetwear buyers.
roots_lines: 2010s: Supreme, Yeezy, Off-White drops; resale culture
Derisive label for buying hype over taste
usage: "He camped out for the drop. Hypebeast."
The world passeth away, and the lust thereof (1Jn 2:17).
Be content with such things as ye have (Heb 13:5).

etymology: From haul, to drag or pull (and a haul, a catch of fish or a thief’s take). Haul videos — creators unboxing and showing off a shopping trip — began on YouTube around 2007–2010 and became a staple genre; TikTok and fast-fashion sites (Shein hauls, from c. 2020) made them shorter and more frequent. "Back-to-school haul," "Target haul," "thrift haul."
biblical_def: In current slang a haul is a shopping trip shown off on camera — a pile of new clothes, makeup, or gadgets unboxed one by one for viewers. Haul videos are among the most-watched genres on youth platforms, and many are paid advertising. The Christian observation: Scripture has a famous haul. Achan, after Jericho, confessed: "When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold... then I coveted them, and took them" (Jos 7:21). See, covet, take, hide — the haul cycle, minus the camera. The haul video trains the same sequence in viewers: see it, want it, buy it. Proverbs says the appetite never closes: "Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied" (Pro 27:20). Jesus answers, "a man’s life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth" (Luk 12:15), and Paul gives the better accounting: "godliness with contentment is great gain" (1Ti 6:6) — and "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Php 4:11). A father can cut the feed and start a family habit: before a purchase, wait a week; after a purchase, give something away. Contentment, Paul says, is learned.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (YouTube c. 2008; TikTok 2020s) for a shopping trip shown off on camera — Achan’s see-covet-take cycle as entertainment; Scripture calls godliness with contentment great gain.
webster_full: HAUL, n. (Gen-Z slang usage, c. 2008–present; YouTube, TikTok) A batch of purchases displayed on video. "Watch my back-to-school haul!"
Haul video; Shein haul, thrift haul, Amazon haul; often sponsored.
Standard senses: a pull; the amount taken at once (a haul of fish, a thief’s haul); a distance travelled ("long haul").

Webster (1828), root word haul: “HAUL, verb transitive 1. To pull or draw with force; to drag; as, to haul a heavy body along on the ground; to haul a boat on shore. haul is equivalent to drag, and differs sometimes from pull and draw, in expressing more force and labor. It is much used by seamen; as, to haul down the sails; haul in the boom; haul aft, etc. 2. To drag;”
Decode for parents: an advertising genre that trains wanting. Teach waiting and giving.
scriptures: Jos 7:21

When I saw among the spoils a goodly Babylonish garment, and two hundred shekels of silver, and a wedge of gold of fifty shekels weight, then I coveted them, and took them; and, behold, they are hid in the earth in the midst of my tent, and the silver under it.
Hell and destruction are never full; so the eyes of man are never satisfied.
And he said unto them, Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth.
But godliness with contentment is great gain.
Php 4:11
Not that I speak in respect of want: for I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content.
corruption_summary: Haul turns acquiring into entertainment and trains viewers in Achan’s cycle — I saw, I coveted, I took; Scripture answers that life does not consist in abundance and that contentment is learned.
corruption_paragraphs: A haul video is an advertisement that does not feel like one. A friendly face shows twenty new things, each "so cute," and the viewer’s eyes do what Proverbs says they always do: they are "never satisfied" (Pro 27:20). The genre has made the act of buying a show and the pile of stuff a kind of achievement.

Achan’s confession is the haul cycle in three verbs: "I saw... I coveted them, and took them" (Jos 7:21). Christ breaks the cycle at the root: life "consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth" (Luk 12:15). Paul says contentment is something he "learned" (Php 4:11). Teach it in your home: wait before buying, give after buying, and turn off the hauls.
roots_summary: French haler (to pull) → English haul, a pull or a catch → c. 2007–2010 YouTube haul videos → 2020s TikTok / fast-fashion hauls.
roots_lines: English haul — a catch of fish; a thief’s take
Often sponsored; a staple influencer genre
usage: "Thirty items in my haul and it was all under $100."
I saw, I coveted, I took (Jos 7:21) — the first haul.
Godliness with contentment is great gain (1Ti 6:6).

etymology: From chronic (Greek chronos, time; of lasting illness) and online. The phrase became a common Twitter and TikTok put-down around 2020–2021, during pandemic lockdowns: a person so immersed in internet culture that his opinions, references, and outrage no longer match how ordinary people think and live. Close kin: "touch grass" (go outside).
biblical_def: In current slang a person is chronically online when the internet has become his world: his jokes need three memes of context, his outrage is about things no one offline has heard of, and his sense of normal comes from a feed. Gen-Z uses it as an insult and, increasingly, as a confession. The Christian observation: the phrase is a diagnosis about time. Scripture tells believers to "walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise, Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:15–16), and Moses prays, "teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom" (Psa 90:12). Hours poured into a feed are days unnumbered. David’s resolution reads like a screen-time policy: "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3). And the slang’s deeper insight is about the mind being shaped by what it consumes; Paul says, "be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind" (Rom 12:2). A chronically online mind has been conformed by an algorithm. A father tells his son: go outside, read a book, sit at a real table, work with your hands; set your affection on things above (Col 3:2), and let God’s Word, not your feed, tell you what is normal.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (Twitter / TikTok, c. 2020–2021) for one so immersed online that his sense of reality is warped — a diagnosis of unredeemed time and a conformed mind.
webster_full: CHRONICALLY ONLINE, adj. phr. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2020–present) So immersed in internet culture as to lose touch with ordinary offline life. "That take is so chronically online."
Used of people, opinions, jokes, and outrage. Often paired with "touch grass."
Also self-applied: "I’m chronically online, I know."

Webster (1828), root word chronic: “CHRONIC, CHRONIC AL, adjective Continuing a long time, as a disease. A chronic disease is one which is inveterate or of long continuance, in distinction from an acute disease, which speedily terminates.”
Decode for parents: your child’s own generation has named the problem. Help him act on the diagnosis.
scriptures: Eph 5:15
See then that ye walk circumspectly, not as fools, but as wise,
Eph 5:16
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil.
So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.
I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes: I hate the work of them that turn aside; it shall not cleave to me.
Rom 12:2
And be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.
corruption_summary: Chronically online diagnoses a mind formed by the feed and days spent unnumbered; Scripture prescribes redeeming the time and a mind renewed by God, not conformed to an algorithm.
corruption_paragraphs: Unusually, this is the culture correcting itself. Young people coined the phrase because they could see what endless scrolling does: it shrinks the world to a feed and makes the feed feel like the world. The opinions it produces are not merely wrong but unreal — outrage at strangers, contempt for ordinary life. Paul’s word for the process is conformity: the mind pressed into the shape of "this world" (Rom 12:2).

Scripture’s remedy is stewardship of time and of the eyes. "Redeeming the time, because the days are evil" (Eph 5:16); "teach us to number our days" (Psa 90:12); "I will set no wicked thing before mine eyes" (Psa 101:3). Turn your child’s own diagnosis into a family practice: phones away at the table, books and work and church in their place.
roots_summary: Greek chronos (time) → chronic, lasting → + online → c. 2020–2021 Twitter / TikTok put-down for internet-warped people and opinions.
roots_lines: Greek chronikos — concerning time; English chronic, of lasting illness
usage: "Getting mad at a cartoon over a meme? That’s chronically online."
Redeeming the time, because the days are evil (Eph 5:16).
Be not conformed, but transformed by the renewing of your mind (Rom 12:2).

etymology: From the plea "pick me!" — a child begging to be chosen. Black Twitter popularized "pick-me" around 2016–2017 ("pick me, choose me, love me," echoing a line from the TV drama Grey’s Anatomy), and TikTok spread "pick-me girl" in 2020–2021 for a young woman who wins male approval by distancing herself from and disparaging other women ("I’m not like other girls"). A "pick-me boy" variant exists.
biblical_def: In current slang a pick-me is someone, usually a girl, who seeks the approval of the opposite sex by putting down her own: "I’m not like other girls, I don’t wear makeup, I just hang out with the guys." The word is an insult, and a sharp one. The Christian observation: the slang has spotted a real sin and then wields it carelessly. The sin is the old one of John 12: "they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God" (Joh 12:43). The pick-me buys favour by self-advertising and by belittling others, and Scripture forbids both: "Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth" (Pro 27:2), and "in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves" (Php 2:3). Paul refused the bargain entirely: "if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ" (Gal 1:10). But the insult is often aimed at girls who are simply different — quieter, plainer, less interested in trends — and that is cruelty, not discernment. Titus 2 offers the better path: older women teaching younger women (Tit 2:3–4), girls bound together rather than competing for boys’ attention. A father tells his daughter: you do not need to be picked; you have been chosen — and the girls around you are sisters to honour, not rivals to undercut.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (Black Twitter c. 2016; TikTok 2020) for one who seeks the opposite sex’s approval by disparaging her own — loving the praise of men; Scripture answers with chosenness in Christ and esteeming others better.
webster_full: PICK-ME, n. / adj. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2016–present) One who seeks the approval of the opposite sex by disparaging others of her own sex. "‘I’m not like other girls’ is such a pick-me line."
Pick-me girl, pick-me boy; pick-me behaviour.
From the plea "pick me, choose me, love me."

Webster (1828), root word pick: “PICK, verb transitive […] 1. To pull off or pluck with the fingers something that grows or adheres to another thing; to separate by the hand, as fruit from trees; as, to pick apples or oranges; to pick strawberries. 2. To pull off or separate with the teeth, beak or claws; as, to pick flesh from a bone; hence, 3.”
Decode for parents: a real vice and a ready insult. Teach your daughter she is chosen, and not to throw the word at the quiet girl.
scriptures: For they loved the praise of men more than the praise of God.
Pro 27:2
Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thine own lips.
Php 2:3
Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves.
Gal 1:10
For do I now persuade men, or God? or do I seek to please men? for if I yet pleased men, I should not be the servant of Christ.
Tit 2:4
That they may teach the young women to be sober, to love their husbands, to love their children,
corruption_summary: Pick-me names the love of men’s praise bought by belittling other women, then becomes a weapon against any girl who is different; Scripture rebukes both the vice and the cruelty.
corruption_paragraphs: The pick-me posture is a small economy of approval: I lower my sisters so that I will look better to the boys. Scripture calls it what it is — loving "the praise of men more than the praise of God" (Joh 12:43) — and gives two commands that undo it: let others praise you (Pro 27:2), and esteem others better than yourself (Php 2:3).

But the slang is also used cruelly. The quiet girl, the girl who prefers fishing to fashion, the girl who will not join the gossip, all get called pick-mes. That is the mean-girl version of the same sin. Paul’s alternative is a community of women teaching and loving one another (Tit 2:3–4). Tell your daughter she does not need to be picked; in Christ she is chosen.
roots_summary: Child’s plea "pick me!" → "pick me, choose me, love me" (TV drama line) → c. 2016 Black Twitter "pick-me" → 2020–2021 TikTok "pick-me girl."
usage: "She said she only has guy friends because girls are ‘too much.’ Pick-me."
They loved the praise of men more than the praise of God (Joh 12:43).
In lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves (Php 2:3).

etymology: From Boomer, short for baby boomer (born c. 1946–1964). "OK boomer" appeared on Reddit and 4chan around 2015 and exploded on TikTok in 2019 as a dismissive reply to an older person’s criticism of the young; in November 2019 New Zealand MP Chlöe Swarbrick used it in Parliament, and it was widely covered as a generational slogan. Used of any older or out-of-touch person regardless of actual birth year.
biblical_def: In current slang OK Boomer is a two-word dismissal of an older person’s opinion: you are old, out of touch, and I do not have to listen. It became a generational slogan in 2019 and is still the reflex reply to a lecture. The Christian observation: Scripture flatly forbids the posture the phrase expresses. "Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD" (Lev 19:32). "Honour thy father and thy mother" is the first commandment with promise (Exo 20:12). "The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness" (Pro 16:31), and "With the ancient is wisdom" (Job 12:12). Scripture also gives the cautionary tale: Rehoboam "forsook the counsel of the old men... and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him" (1Ki 12:8), and lost ten tribes in a day. That is OK Boomer as foreign policy. Paul does not say elders are always right; he says how to disagree: "Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father" (1Ti 5:1). A father tells his son: you may think Grandpa is wrong about something, and you may be right; you must still stand up when he enters, listen to the end, and answer him as a son. Every generation gets old; the one that mocks its elders is training its own children.
webster_summary: Gen-Z slang (Reddit c. 2015; TikTok 2019) dismissing an older person’s view as out of touch — contempt for the hoary head that Scripture forbids; Rehoboam’s error in two words.
webster_full: OK BOOMER, interj. (Gen-Z slang, c. 2015; viral 2019) A dismissive retort to an older person’s criticism or advice, implying he is out of touch. "Phones are ruining your generation." "OK boomer."
Applied to any older or old-fashioned person, regardless of birth year.
Boomer: a member of the baby-boom generation (born c. 1946–1964).

Webster (1828), root word boom: “BOOM, verb intransitive 1. In marine language, to rush with violence, as a ship under a press of sail. 2. To swell; to roll and roar, as waves. The hoarse waves booming to the ocean shore. 3. To cry as the bittern. The Dutch use bom for the sound of an empty barrel, and bommen is to drum.”
Decode for parents: generational contempt in two words. Do not answer contempt with contempt; teach honour.
scriptures: Thou shalt rise up before the hoary head, and honour the face of the old man, and fear thy God: I am the LORD.
Honour thy father and thy mother: that thy days may be long upon the land which the LORD thy God giveth thee.
The hoary head is a crown of glory, if it be found in the way of righteousness.
But he forsook the counsel of the old men, which they had given him, and consulted with the young men that were grown up with him, and which stood before him:
Rebuke not an elder, but intreat him as a father; and the younger men as brethren;
corruption_summary: OK Boomer turns age into a reason not to listen; Scripture commands rising before the hoary head, shows Rehoboam’s ruin, and teaches the young to entreat elders as fathers even in disagreement.
corruption_paragraphs: Every generation has had its grievances with the one before; the novelty of "OK boomer" is that it refuses even to argue. It answers an elder not with reasons but with his birth year. Scripture calls that dishonour, and treats honour of the aged as part of the fear of God: "rise up before the hoary head... and fear thy God: I am the LORD" (Lev 19:32).

Rehoboam is the Bible’s case study. He heard the old men, dismissed them, took counsel of his peers, and split the kingdom (1Ki 12:8). The young are not told elders are infallible; they are told how to disagree: "intreat him as a father" (1Ti 5:1). Parents should also listen: the phrase is sometimes a cry from young people who feel unheard. Answer it by listening first, and by modelling the honour you hope to receive.
roots_summary: Baby boom (post-1945 birth surge) → boomer → c. 2015 Reddit "OK boomer" → 2019 TikTok and New Zealand Parliament → general dismissal of older people.
roots_lines: Imitative boom — a deep sound; a sudden surge
2019: TikTok surge; used in New Zealand Parliament
Now any dismissal of an older or old-fashioned view
usage: "Grandpa said to get off my phone. OK boomer."
Rise up before the hoary head (Lev 19:32).
Rehoboam forsook the counsel of the old men (1Ki 12:8).
